# Postmortem: October 2026 OIDC login failures

On 2 October 2026 between 14:02 and 14:19 UTC, roughly 9 percent of OIDC logins
failed with an invalid grant error. Password logins and workload identity were
unaffected.

OidcBroker rejected refresh-token requests from one identity provider because
the broker host clock had drifted 47 seconds behind. The access token lifetime
was not the issue; the refresh request itself carried a timestamp the provider
considered too old.

The broker hosts now run an authenticated time service, and refresh requests are
retried once on a clock-skew error before failing the login.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-10-oidc
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: October 2026 OIDC login failures

row.content:
# Audit trail

Every credential read, permission change, and pipeline deployment writes an
AuditTrail entry. Entries are append-only and are retained in the active
store for 400 days, after which they are archived to cold storage; archived
entries remain queryable through the `quorva audit` command.

Each entry carries at least the actor identity, the resource, the action, and
a digest of the request body; some authentication methods add their own
identifiers. Request bodies themselves are never stored.
row.name: qrv-guide-audit-log

row.content:
# Japan region (ap-northeast-1)

The ap-northeast-1 region serves Japanese customers from two availability
zones. The latency SLA is p95 150 ms for in-region requests. Data residency is
Japan: payloads, indexes, and backups stay in the region. Default retention for
stored records is 45 days.

The regional edge endpoint is quorva-edge-jp, and it terminates TLS for all
regional traffic.
row.name: qrv-region-jp

row.content:
# quorva status

`quorva status` lists running pipelines and, with `--verbose`, each stage's
last error, restart count, and current offset. It reads the fleet's control
plane, not the data plane, so it is cheap to poll. For per-stage record counts
and timing, see the metrics endpoint rather than status.
row.name: qrv-cli-status

# Deployment FAQ

Do I need to validate the pipeline configuration before deploying? The runner
re-validates. Can I deploy without validating the pipeline configuration first?
Not recommended. Where is the pipeline configuration validated before deploy?
In CI and at startup. What validates the pipeline configuration on deploy? The
control plane. Is deploy-time configuration validation strict? Yes.
row.name: qrv-deploy-faq

row.content:
# US region (us-east-1)

The us-east-1 region serves North American customers from three availability
zones. The latency SLA is p95 80 ms for in-region requests. Data residency is
the United States: payloads, indexes, and backups stay in the region. Default
retention for stored records is 30 days.

The regional edge endpoint is quorva-edge-us, and it terminates TLS for all
regional traffic.
row.name: qrv-region-us

row.content:
# Attaching sinks (v2)

Quorva v2 replaces `add_sink()` with the `.to(...)` operator:
`pipeline.to(sink_a).to(sink_b)` attaches sinks left to right, returning the
pipeline so calls chain. `.to()` exists only in v2; v1 code using `add_sink`
keeps working under 2.x with a deprecation warning until 3.0.
row.name: qrv-v2-sinks

row.content:
# Installation

Quorva supports Python 3.11 through 3.13. Install the base package with
`pip install quorva`. Connector extras are installed per backend, for example
`pip install 'quorva[postgres]'` or `quorva[s3]`. The CLI ships with the base
package. Pin the minor version in production; the on-disk checkpoint format is
stable within a minor release.
row.name: qrv-install

row.content:
# Pub/Sub sink

The Pub/Sub sink publishes records to a topic. Delivery is at-least-once by
default; exactly-once delivery is available only when the subscription is
created with that option. Ordering is preserved when the publish carries an
ordering key.

The maximum message size is 10 MiB. Default retention is 7 days, after which an
unacknowledged message is dropped.
row.name: qrv-sink-pubsub

row.content:
# PostgresSink API reference

`qv.sinks.PostgresSink(dsn, table, *, flush_interval_ms=250, batch_rows=500,
idempotent=True)`. Buffered rows are flushed when either `batch_rows` is
reached or `flush_interval_ms` elapses, whichever comes first; the default
flush interval is 250 milliseconds. `idempotent=True` declares writes safe to
retry, which lets the runner re-submit a batch after a transient failure.
row.name: qrv-sink-postgres

row.content:
# JSONL source

`qv.sources.JsonlSource(path)` reads newline-delimited JSON, one record per
line, with the line number as offset. Malformed lines route to dead-letter
handling when configured rather than stopping the run.
row.name: qrv-source-jsonl

row.content:
# Supplying credentials from the environment

Connectors resolve credentials from the process environment before reading any
file: set `QUORVA_API_KEY`, or for OAuth `QUORVA_CLIENT_ID` and
`QUORVA_CLIENT_SECRET`. On fleet runners, workload identity is preferred: the
runner exchanges its platform identity for a Quorva token at startup, and no
secret is written to configuration or disk at all.
row.name: qrv-auth-env
row.source_description: bench corpus: Supplying credentials from the environment

row.content:
# Postmortem: November 2026 quota rejections

On 4 November 2026 a tenant saw `quota_exceeded` rejections on three pipelines
for 12 minutes. All three pipelines shared one pipeline group, so a single
TenantQuota limit covered them, and their combined in-flight batches exceeded
that limit while most of the batches sat unacknowledged behind a slow sink.
Raising the per-pipeline limit had no effect because the binding constraint
was the per-group tenant quota.

The fix adds a warning when one pipeline in a group accounts for more than 60%
of the group's in-flight batches.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-11-quota
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: November 2026 quota rejections

row.content:
# Troubleshooting common failures

Start with `quorva status --verbose`, which reports each stage's last error and
restart count. A pipeline that starts and then stalls is usually waiting on a
slow sink or an exhausted connection pool. A pipeline that fails at startup is
usually a configuration problem: run `quorva validate` and read the first
error, not the last.
row.name: qrv-troubleshooting

row.content:
# Postmortem: March 2026 duplicate backfill

On 17 March 2026 a BackfillPlan run over a 90-day range wrote 14,000 duplicate
records to a transactional sink. The requested range ended two hours after the
watermark, but the plan had been started with the overlap check disabled by an
operator flag.

The sink's idempotency keys covered live writes but not backfill segments, so
the duplicates were not collapsed. The fix removes the override flag so an
overlapping range cannot start, and gives each backfill segment its own
idempotency namespace so a retried segment collapses instead of duplicating.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-03-backfill
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: March 2026 duplicate backfill

row.content:
# Postmortem: January 2026 credential expiry

On 19 January 2026 a long-running pipeline failed every batch from 08:41 to
09:07 UTC
with authentication errors. The credential file had been rotated at 08:40, but
the pipeline was configured for ephemeral runs, so the SecretRotationJob was not
active and the in-memory credential remained the expired one. Restarting the
pipeline picked up the new version.

The fix makes validation warn when a long-running ephemeral pipeline uses a
file-backed credential. The re-read interval was not the cause.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-01-secret
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: January 2026 credential expiry

row.content:
# Blue/green deployment cutover

The CutoverController shifts traffic between blue and green fleets in steps
controlled by `cutover_step_percent`, which defaults to 10 percent. Each step
is held for `cutover_hold_s` (default 300 seconds) while error rate and p99
latency are compared against the stable fleet.

A step is rolled back automatically when the new fleet's error rate exceeds
the stable fleet's by more than 2 percentage points.
row.name: qrv-guide-cutover

row.content:
# The record model

Records are plain dictionaries with JSON-compatible values plus a small
envelope the runner stamps: a `trace_id` set at the source, the source offset,
and the arrival timestamp. Transforms see the payload; the envelope travels
alongside. Keep payloads flat where you can -- deeply nested records cost more
to serialize between stages.
row.name: qrv-record-model

row.content:
# Tenant quotas

The TenantQuota limit is enforced per pipeline group at the sink: a tenant may
have at most 32 in-flight batches across the pipelines in one group. When the
limit is reached, producers block for up to `quota_wait_s`, which defaults to
20 seconds, before the batch is rejected as `quota_exceeded`.

A single pipeline may hold at most 16 in-flight batches. The group limit
applies to their sum, so the tenant quota caps the effective in-flight count
below the fleet worker's 64-batch capacity.

Quota consumption is released when the sink acknowledges the batch, not when
the batch is produced.
row.name: qrv-guide-quotas

row.content:
# Deploying with the CLI

`quorva deploy pipeline.yaml --fleet prod` validates the pipeline, uploads it,
and starts it on the named fleet. `--watch` tails the rollout; `--dry-run`
stops after validation. The CLI reads fleet credentials from your console
session (`quorva login`). Roll back with `quorva deploy --revision N`.
row.name: qrv-cli-deploy
row.source_description: bench corpus: Deploying with the CLI

# Security advisory: CertificateAuthority intermediate rotation

The intermediate certificate used by CertificateAuthority will be rotated on
1 December 2026. Clients that pin the current intermediate will fail the
handshake once the old certificate is retired, seven days after the rotation.

Your client certificates are unaffected by the rotation itself. You only need to trust the new intermediate before the retirement date.
The root certificate does not change.

The new intermediate is published through the usual trust bundle.
row.name: qrv-security-advisory-ca
row.source_description: bench corpus: Security advisory: CertificateAuthority intermediate rotation

row.content:
# Performance tuning FAQ

Does a larger batch size improve write throughput for the Postgres sink? It
depends. Does batch size affect latency as well as throughput? Yes, indirectly.
Can I change the batch size per environment? See configuration. Is there a
recommended batch size for high-throughput Postgres writes? Contact support.
Why did my write throughput drop after I increased batch size? Open an issue.
row.name: qrv-tuning-faq

row.content:
# S3 source

`qv.sources.S3Source(bucket, prefix, *, format="auto")` reads objects from an
S3 bucket into the pipeline, tracking the last fully-read object as its
offset. New objects under the prefix are picked up on each poll. Use the
`since` parameter to skip historical objects on first run. Formats are
inferred from object suffixes unless pinned.
row.name: qrv-source-s3

row.content:
# Workload identity authentication

Workload identity lets a service authenticate with the platform instead of a
shared secret. WorkloadIdentity issues an access token valid for 1 hour when the
process starts, and the token rotates automatically on every restart; there is
no manual rotation step.

Audit records store the spiffe_id of the calling workload.
row.name: qrv-auth-workload

row.content:
# Quickstart

Install the SDK, define a pipeline, and run it locally in under five minutes.
A pipeline connects a source to a sink through zero or more transforms. This
page walks through reading a CSV file and loading it into a local DuckDB table,
then points at the deployment guide for anything beyond your laptop.
row.name: qrv-quickstart

row.content:
# Authentication FAQ

How do I authenticate the webhook sink with an API key? See the connector docs.
Can the webhook sink use an API key and OAuth together? No. Where does the
webhook sink read the API key from? The credentials block. Does an API key for
the webhook sink expire? Keys do not expire. Is the webhook sink API key
logged? Never.
row.name: qrv-auth-faq

row.content:
# Postmortem: August 2026 sink CPU saturation

On 22 August 2026 between 10:12 and 11:48 UTC, a fleet pipeline's sink workers
reached 94% CPU. The CodecNegotiator had downgraded batches to gzip because the
sink advertised no zstd support; gzip's decompression cost more CPU per byte
than zstd, and the team had assumed the two were comparable. Throughput fell
by 38%.

The fix adds a `compression.min_throughput_mbps` warning when a downgraded
codec is in use.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-08-compression
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: August 2026 sink CPU saturation

row.content:
# APAC region (ap-southeast-2)

The ap-southeast-2 region serves Asia Pacific customers from two availability
zones. The latency SLA is p95 180 ms for in-region requests. Data residency is
Asia Pacific: payloads, indexes, and backups stay in the region. Default
retention for stored records is 45 days.

The regional edge endpoint is quorva-edge-ap, and it terminates TLS for all
regional traffic.
row.name: qrv-region-ap

row.content:
# Postmortem: May 2026 EU edge outage

On 3 May 2026 quorva-edge-eu refused new TLS connections for 22 minutes. The
region behind the edge stayed healthy, but every request that entered through
the edge failed.

The cause was an expired TLS certificate. The rotation job that renews the edge
certificate had been disabled during a maintenance window and was never
re-enabled, so the certificate expired at 06:00 UTC.

Rotation is now monitored, and an expiring certificate pages the on-call owner
seven days ahead.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-05-eu
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: May 2026 EU edge outage

row.content:
# Batches and buffers

Stages exchange records in batches through bounded buffers owned by the runner.
Batch size is a per-sink tuning knob, not a global; buffers have high- and
low-water marks that drive flow control. A batch is the unit of retry and of
dead-lettering: a failure routes the whole batch, not a single record.
row.name: qrv-batch-model

row.content:
# Idempotent writes

A sink is idempotent when applying the same batch twice has the same effect as
applying it once -- achieved with insert IDs, upserts on a key, or a
transactional commit. The runner only retries writes a sink declares
idempotent; for the rest it uses a two-phase commit where the backend allows,
and otherwise routes an uncertain batch to dead-letter rather than risk a
duplicate.
row.name: qrv-guide-idempotency

row.content:
# Ephemeral runs: executing without persisted state

For backfills and tests where resuming is pointless, disable state persistence
entirely: pass `state_uri=None` to `qv.execute`, or set `checkpoint_store_uri:
none` in quorva.yaml. The runner keeps offsets in memory for the life of the
process and writes nothing to the state store; a crash means the run starts
over. Combine with `limit` to bound reprocessing.
row.name: qrv-howto-ephemeral
row.source_description: bench corpus: Ephemeral runs: executing without persisted state

row.content:
# Metrics and logging

The runner exports per-stage counters (records in, records out, bytes written,
retries attempted) and timing histograms over a Prometheus endpoint. Logs are
structured JSON by default; set `log_format: text` for human-readable output.
Correlate a record's path through the pipeline with the `trace_id` field
stamped at the source.
row.name: qrv-observability

row.content:
# Postmortem: July 2026 Kafka duplicates

On 19 July 2026 a consumer group rebalance caused duplicated records in one
Kafka topic for about six minutes. KafkaPublisher retried a batch whose publish
had actually succeeded, and because the destination consumer was not idempotent,
the retry was visible downstream.

The duplicate is within the transport contract described by the Kafka sink, so
the remediation is on the consumer side: consumers now record and discard batches
they have already processed. No records were lost.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-07-kafka
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: July 2026 Kafka duplicates

row.content:
# Record ordering

Within a single source partition, records keep their arrival order all the way
to the sink: the runner does not reorder a stage's output. Across partitions
there is no global order -- two records from different partitions may be written
in either sequence. Transforms that need to compare neighbouring records should
rely on the within-partition guarantee, not on a global one.
row.name: qrv-guide-ordering

row.content:
# Writing transforms

A transform is a Python callable registered with `@qv.transform`. It receives a
batch of records and returns the transformed batch; raising drops the batch
into the retry path. Keep transforms pure -- the runner may re-execute a batch
after a recovery, and a transform with side effects will repeat them.
row.name: qrv-transforms

row.content:
# Postgres source (CDC)

`qv.sources.PostgresSource(dsn, *, slot, tables)` streams a Postgres database's
changes into the pipeline by reading its logical-replication slot -- inserts,
updates and deletes as they commit. Its offset is the log position, so a run
resumes without re-reading the table. This is for ingesting *from* Postgres;
writing pipeline output *to* Postgres is the Postgres sink.
row.name: qrv-source-postgres

row.content:
# Postmortem: April 2026 late-data loss

On 2 April 2026 between 14:03 and 15:26 UTC, one pipeline lost records that
had arrived on time but were emitted late by a transform's output buffer.
The pipeline used the default watermark delay, but the transform buffered
output for 90 seconds, so records stamped just before the buffered flush
were already below the watermark when they reached the sink stage.

The WatermarkTracker was behaving as documented; the loss came from the
transform's buffer exceeding the watermark delay. The pipeline had no
consumer for the late-data side output, so the records routed there were
discarded rather than delivered. The fix caps transform buffering at half
the watermark delay and fails validation when a transform declares a longer
buffer. No change was made to the checkpoint warning.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-04-watermark
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: April 2026 late-data loss

row.content:
# DuckDB sink

`qv.sinks.DuckDbSink(path, table)` writes pipeline output to a local DuckDB
file -- the default sink in the quickstart because it needs no server. Writes
are transactional per batch, so they are safe to retry.
row.name: qrv-sink-duckdb

row.content:
# Authenticating with OAuth service accounts

Create a service account in the Quorva console, grant it the pipeline-runner
role, and download its client credentials. Reference the credentials file from
the connector, or exchange it yourself: POST the client id and secret to
`/oauth/token` and pass the returned bearer token in the `Authorization`
header. Tokens expire after one hour; the SDK refreshes them automatically
before expiry.
row.name: qrv-auth-oauth
row.source_description: bench corpus: Authenticating with OAuth service accounts

row.content:
# Defining a pipeline

A pipeline is declared in quorva.yaml as a `source`, an ordered list of
`transforms`, and one or more `sinks`, or built in Python by composing
`qv.Source`, `qv.transform` callables, and `qv.Sink` objects. The runner wires
them into a stage graph. Every pipeline needs a unique `name`, used for state
scoping and status reporting.
row.name: qrv-pipeline-basics

row.content:
# Postmortem: September 2026 APAC latency breach

On 8 September 2026 the APAC region breached its p95 latency SLA for 41
minutes. quorva-edge-ap kept serving traffic, but p95 reached 310 ms.

The trigger was a zone failure in the APAC region. Traffic failed over to
ap-northeast-1, and the cross-region hop added roughly 130 ms per request. The
breach was a direct consequence of the failover path rather than of any change
in the service.

The runbook now records the failover latency budget, and alerts on the
region-level p95 rather than only on error rate.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-09-ap
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: September 2026 APAC latency breach

row.content:
# EU region (eu-west-1)

The eu-west-1 region serves European customers from three availability zones.
The latency SLA is p95 120 ms for in-region requests. Data residency is
in-region only: payloads, indexes, and backups never leave the region. Default
retention for stored records is 30 days.

The regional edge endpoint is quorva-edge-eu, and it terminates TLS for all
regional traffic.
row.name: qrv-region-eu

row.content:
# Glossary

**DLQ** -- dead-letter queue; where records that exhaust their retries are
routed. **QPS** -- queries per second; used when talking about API rate
limits. **Watermark** -- the timestamp up to which a source's input is
considered complete. **Runner** -- the process that executes pipeline stages.
**Offset** -- a source's resumable position in its input.
row.name: qrv-glossary

row.content:
# Programmatic deployment

Fleets expose a REST deployment endpoint for CI systems and anything else that
cannot shell out: PUT the rendered pipeline definition to
`/fleets/{fleet}/pipelines/{name}` with a service-account bearer token. The
response carries the revision number; GET the same path for rollout status.
The SDK wraps this as `qv.fleet.deploy(pipeline, fleet=...)`.
row.name: qrv-deploy-api

row.content:
# Error code index

QRV-1001 invalid pipeline file. QRV-1002 unknown stage name. QRV-2003 source
connection refused. QRV-2004 source credentials rejected. QRV-3001 transform
raised. QRV-3002 transform timeout. QRV-4010 sink connection refused. QRV-4011
sink credentials rejected. QRV-4012 sink write rejected. QRV-4013 sink
timeout. QRV-5001 state store unavailable. QRV-5002 checkpoint corrupt.
row.name: qrv-err-index

row.content:
# Configuring sinks (v1)

In Quorva v1 a sink is attached by calling `pipeline.add_sink(sink)` after
construction; multiple calls add multiple sinks, applied in call order. The
`add_sink` method is maintained on the 1.x line but is not available in v2,
where sinks are attached with the `.to(...)` operator instead.
row.name: qrv-v1-sinks

row.content:
# S3 sink

`qv.sinks.S3Sink(bucket, prefix, *, format="parquet", batch_bytes=64_000_000)`
writes pipeline output to an S3 bucket as size-bounded objects under the given
prefix. Object names embed the stage, window, and batch sequence so a replay
overwrites rather than duplicates. Formats: parquet, jsonl, csv. Credentials
come from the standard provider chain or the connector's `credentials` block.
row.name: qrv-sink-s3

row.content:
# Environment-variable overrides

Any quorva.yaml scalar can be overridden from the environment with the
`QUORVA_` prefix and the uppercased dotted path: `QUORVA_COMMIT_INTERVAL_S=10`
overrides `commit_interval_s`. Overrides are read once at startup. This is for
deployment-specific values; connector credentials have their own resolution
order (environment, then file, then workload identity).
row.name: qrv-config-env

row.content:
# Ephemeral mode

Ephemeral mode disables checkpoints. It is selected by setting
`checkpoint_store_uri: none` (or `state_uri: None` in the Python API), matching
the how-to on ephemeral runs. In this mode the checkpoint interval is not
applicable, the in-flight batch cap is 4, and the memory ceiling is 256 MiB.

Every run starts again from the source offsets, so the same range can be
executed more than once. EphemeralMode is the runtime flag that records this
choice in the configuration dump.
row.name: qrv-runner-ephemeral

row.content:
# quorva run (local execution)

`quorva run pipeline.yaml` executes a pipeline on the local machine, in the
current process, with no fleet involved. It is the inner-loop command: fast to
start, logs to the terminal, and honours `--limit` and `--state-uri`. Use it
for development and backfills; `quorva deploy` is for putting a pipeline on a
runner fleet in production.
row.name: qrv-cli-run

row.content:
# Local runner (embedded)

The local runner is the `runner: local` option; it executes the pipeline inside
the CLI process, which is what `quorva run` does without a deployment. Its
checkpoint interval is 30 seconds, the in-flight batch cap is 8, and the memory
ceiling is 512 MiB. The pipeline-level `commit_interval_s` default applies
unchanged.

A failed batch is retried in place by the local runner. Batch assignment is
handled by EmbeddedScheduler, which always takes the oldest queued batch first
and never preempts a batch that is already in flight.
row.name: qrv-runner-embedded

row.content:
# QRV-4012: sink write rejected

Raised when a sink rejects a batch because the record schema does not match the
destination's declared schema. Common causes: a column added upstream that the
destination table lacks, or a type widening (int to float) the destination
refuses. The failing batch is routed to dead-letter handling if configured;
otherwise the pipeline stops. Fix the destination schema or add a transform
that projects the record onto the destination's columns, then resume the run.
row.name: qrv-err-4012
row.source_description: bench corpus: QRV-4012: sink write rejected

row.content:
# Schema validation

Enable validation on a source with `schema: {mode: enforce, ref:
schemas/orders.json}`. In `enforce` mode a non-conforming record fails its
batch; in `warn` mode it is counted and logged but passed through. Schemas are
JSON Schema draft 2020-12; the reference may point at a file or an inline
definition. Validation runs before the first transform, so transforms can rely
on the declared shape.
row.name: qrv-guide-schema

row.content:
# Rate limits

The ingest API accepts 1,000 requests per second per organization, measured
over a sliding ten-second window; bursts above the limit receive HTTP 429 with
a Retry-After header. Pipeline traffic through connectors is not subject to
this limit -- it applies to the REST ingest endpoint only. Contact support to
raise the ceiling for sustained high-volume ingest.
row.name: qrv-guide-rate-limits

row.content:
# Fleet runner

The fleet runner is the `runner: fleet` option; it distributes a pipeline
across several workers in one cluster. In fleet mode the checkpoint interval
defaults to 10 seconds, overriding the pipeline-level `commit_interval_s`
default of 30 seconds. Each worker may hold up to 64 in-flight batches and is
limited to a 2 GiB memory ceiling.

A worker loss reassigns that worker's in-flight batches to another worker, so
those batches execute a second time. The delivery and idempotency guides describe how a transactional sink or
dead-letter routing keeps such a replay from reaching the destination twice. Workers coordinate through RunnerLease, which renews
every 5 seconds.
row.name: qrv-runner-fleet

row.content:
# Sinks overview

Built-in sinks cover object stores, relational databases, and webhooks. Sinks
declare whether writes are idempotent; the runner uses the declaration to
decide what it may safely retry after a failure. Custom sinks subclass
`qv.Sink` and implement `write_batch`.
row.name: qrv-sinks-overview

row.content:
# Testing pipelines

`qv.testing` provides `MemorySource` and `MemorySink` for wiring a pipeline
against in-memory data, and `FlakySink`, which fails a configurable fraction of
batches to exercise retry and dead-letter paths. Tests run the pipeline with
`qv.execute(..., state_uri=None)` so no state is persisted.
row.name: qrv-testing

row.content:
# Connectors

Connectors are the installable source and sink backends. Install the ones you
need as extras: `pip install 'quorva[postgres,s3]'`. Each connector declares
its capabilities -- offset tracking for sources, write idempotency for sinks --
which the runner reads to decide what it may safely retry or resume.
row.name: qrv-connectors-overview

row.content:
# Migrating from v1 to v2

Replace `Pipeline(...).run(...)` with `qv.execute(Pipeline(...), ...)`:
`blocking` becomes `wait`, `max_records` becomes `limit`, and `state_dir`
becomes `state_uri` (prefix the old path with `file://`). `run()` returned
None; `qv.execute` returns a RunHandle, so code that polled logs for completion
can call `wait()` instead. The v1 method keeps working under 2.x with a
deprecation warning until 3.0.
row.name: qrv-migration

row.content:
# Performance basics

Throughput is governed by the slowest stage and by batch size at the sinks;
latency by the commit interval and buffer depth. Measure with the per-stage
counters before tuning. Scaling workers helps when stages are independent; it
does nothing for a single saturated sink, which wants a larger batch instead.
row.name: qrv-performance-overview

row.content:
# Retry policy

Transient failures are retried per stage with exponential backoff: `retries:
{max_attempts: 5, base_delay_ms: 100, max_delay_ms: 30000, jitter: true}`.
Only failures the connector marks retryable are attempted again; a schema
rejection is not, a timeout is. A batch that exhausts its attempts is handed
to dead-letter handling when configured. Tune `max_attempts` down for
latency-sensitive pipelines rather than disabling retries outright.
row.name: qrv-guide-retries

row.content:
# Parquet source

`qv.sources.ParquetSource(path)` reads Parquet row groups into records. It is
the fastest file source for columnar data and preserves types without the
inference CSV needs. Offsets are (file, row-group) pairs.
row.name: qrv-source-parquet

row.content:
# OIDC authentication

OIDC authentication is for interactive and CI clients that already have an
identity provider. OidcBroker exchanges an authorization code for an access
token, and the token lifetime is 10 minutes. OidcBroker rotates the token
through the refresh token before it expires, so a long-running job does not see
a gap.

Audit records store the sub claim of the authenticated principal.
row.name: qrv-auth-oidc

row.content:
# Glossary (extended)

**CDC** -- change data capture; reading a database's commit log as a stream.
**2PC** -- two-phase commit; a protocol for atomic writes across systems.
**RPS** -- requests per second, used interchangeably with QPS for rate limits.
**Tail latency** -- high-percentile (p95/p99) latency, the slow requests.
**Backfill** -- reprocessing historical input, usually as an ephemeral run.
row.name: qrv-glossary-ext

row.content:
# Local development loop

The fast loop is edit, `quorva validate`, `quorva run --limit 1000` against a
sample, read the terminal logs. Keep a small fixture file next to the pipeline
so a run needs no network. Switch the sink to DuckDB locally and to the real
destination only in the deployed config.
row.name: qrv-local-dev

row.content:
# Postmortem: February 2026 fleet stalls

On 11 February 2026 between 09:14 and 09:52 UTC, fleet pipelines paused and
resumed repeatedly. A batch that had completed was executed a second time by a
different worker, and sinks without idempotent writes saw duplicates.

The coordinator was not observing RunnerLease renewals. A renewal recorded while
the worker was writing a checkpoint was compared against the checkpoint marker
instead of the lease table, so a healthy worker looked gone and its batches were
reassigned.

The fix serialises renewals with checkpoint writes and compares against the lease
table only. The renewal period itself is unchanged.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-02-lease
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: February 2026 fleet stalls

row.content:
# Postmortem: June 2026 full resnapshots

On 8 June 2026 four PostgresSource pipelines restarted with a full snapshot
rather than resuming from their replication slot. The pipelines had been
paused for maintenance for 31 hours, so their slots had been released and the
database had already reclaimed their WAL.

No data was lost, because the snapshot restored the table state, but the
snapshot took 41 minutes and doubled replica load. The fix requires an
explicit `cdc_pause_acknowledged: true` before a pause longer than the
retention window is planned.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-06-cdc
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: June 2026 full resnapshots

row.content:
# Kafka sink

The Kafka sink publishes records through KafkaPublisher. Delivery is
at-least-once: a failed publish is retried, and a consumer may see a duplicate.
Ordering is preserved per partition, and records with the same key always land in
the same partition.

Retention is configured on the broker, not by the sink. The maximum message
size is 1 MiB, and a larger record fails the batch.
row.name: qrv-sink-kafka

row.content:
# Backfilling historical ranges

A BackfillPlan splits a requested date range into segments of at most 6 hours
and runs them at `backfill_concurrency`, which defaults to 2. Each segment is
checkpointed independently, so a failed segment resumes without restarting
completed ones; a managed plan therefore never runs in ephemeral mode, though
an ad-hoc backfill outside a plan may.

The plan refuses to start when the target sink's current watermark overlaps
the requested range, because the replay would duplicate live records.
row.name: qrv-guide-backfill

row.content:
# Compression codecs

Batch payloads are compressed with `compression.codec`, which defaults to
`zstd` at level 3. The CodecNegotiator chooses the highest level both ends
advertise; a sink that advertises only `gzip` downgrades the batch to gzip
level 6 and logs once per run.

Compression is applied after batching and before encryption. The negotiated
codec is recorded in the batch header for the sink.
row.name: qrv-guide-compression

row.content:
# Dead-letter handling

A record that keeps failing -- its batch has exhausted the retry policy -- is
routed to the pipeline's dead-letter destination instead of stopping the run.
Configure it with `on_error: dead-letter` and a `dead_letter_uri` pointing at a
file, object-store prefix, or table. Each routed record carries the original
payload, the failing stage, the final error, and the attempt count, so the
batch can be inspected and replayed later with `quorva replay`.
row.name: qrv-guide-dlq

row.content:
# Watermarks and late data

The WatermarkTracker records, per partition, the highest event time seen
and subtracts a configurable delay to form the pipeline watermark. The
default `watermark_delay_s` is 30 seconds; the minimum accepted value is 5
seconds. Records whose event time is below the watermark are routed to the
late-data side output rather than dropped.

The tracker embeds the watermark in every state checkpoint, so a restart
resumes from the last committed position instead of replaying the whole
window, and it emits a `watermark_lag` gauge every 10 batches. A watermark
that does not advance for 20 consecutive checkpoints is logged at WARN
level.
row.name: qrv-guide-watermarks
row.source_description: bench corpus: Watermarks and late data

row.content:
# quorva validate

`quorva validate pipeline.yaml` parses the pipeline file, resolves every stage
name against the registry, type-checks the source/transform/sink wiring, and
reports the first error with its line. It makes no network calls and touches
no state, so it is safe to run in CI. A clean validate is a precondition the
runner re-checks at startup anyway.
row.name: qrv-cli-validate

row.content:
# Architecture overview

A Quorva pipeline is a directed graph of stages executed by the runner. Sources
produce records, transforms map or filter them, and sinks write them out.
Stages exchange records through bounded buffers owned by the runner. State --
offsets, watermarks, and in-flight batches -- is tracked per stage and persisted
by the state store between runs.
row.name: qrv-architecture

row.content:
# Security advisory: AuditTrail digest format

On 1 December 2026 the AuditTrail digest changes from a SHA-256 digest
truncated to 128 bits to the full 256-bit digest. Entries written before that
date remain verifiable with the old format and are not rewritten.

Verification tools must accept both formats; an entry whose digest length
matches neither format is rejected. The retention period is unaffected.
row.name: qrv-security-advisory-audit
row.source_description: bench corpus: Security advisory: AuditTrail digest format

row.content:
# CLI overview

The `quorva` command wraps the common lifecycle: `quorva validate` checks a
pipeline file, `quorva run` executes it locally, `quorva deploy` submits it to
a runner fleet, and `quorva status` reports on running pipelines. Every
subcommand takes `--config` to point at a quorva.yaml other than the one in the
working directory.
row.name: qrv-cli-overview

row.content:
# Rotating connector secrets

File-backed connector secrets are read from a referenced credential file at
pipeline start and held in memory for the lifetime of the run. The
SecretRotationJob re-reads the file every 15 minutes and swaps a credential
in place when its version changes, without restarting the pipeline.

A swap takes effect from the next batch onward; in-flight batches keep the
old credential. Rotation is refused while a checkpoint write is in progress,
so a swap can be delayed by up to one checkpoint interval. Pipelines running
in ephemeral mode do not start the job.
row.name: qrv-guide-secret-rotation

row.content:
# Running pipelines (v1)

In Quorva v1, construct a `Pipeline` and call its `run()` method:
`Pipeline(source, transforms, sink).run(blocking=True)`. `run()` takes
`blocking`, `max_records`, and `state_dir`. The v1 API is maintained for the
1.x line but receives no new features; new projects should start on v2.
row.name: qrv-v1-run

row.content:
# QRV-5002: checkpoint corrupt

Raised at startup when the state store holds a checkpoint the runner cannot
parse -- usually a checkpoint written by a different Quorva minor version, or a
partially-written file left by a killed process. The run refuses to start
rather than reprocess from an unknown position. Resolve by pointing
`checkpoint_store_uri` at a fresh location to start clean, or restoring a known
-good checkpoint; there is no in-place repair.
row.name: qrv-err-5002

row.content:
# Checkpointing pipeline state

The runner persists each stage's offsets and watermarks to the state store at
every commit interval. After a crash or redeploy, the pipeline resumes from the
last committed state instead of reprocessing its input from the beginning.
Point the state store at durable storage with the `checkpoint_store_uri` key in
quorva.yaml; the default commit interval is 30 seconds, tunable per pipeline
with `commit_interval_s`.
row.name: qrv-guide-checkpointing

row.content:
# Frequently asked questions

Is schema validation available on the free tier? Contact your account team.
Does schema validation affect billing? See the pricing page. Can schema
validation be enabled per environment? Reach out to support with your org id.
Where do I report a schema validation bug? The issue tracker. Is there a
schema validation roadmap? Watch the public milestones page.
row.name: qrv-faq

row.content:
# HTTP polling source

`qv.sources.HttpSource(url, *, interval_s=60, cursor_param="since")` polls an
HTTP endpoint on an interval and emits the returned items, advancing a cursor
it passes back on the next poll. Use it for APIs without a streaming feed.
row.name: qrv-source-http
qrv-auth-apikey
row.source_description: bench corpus: Authenticating with API keys

row.content:
# quorva.yaml reference

Top-level keys: `name` -- pipeline name, required. `runner` -- local or fleet.
`checkpoint_store_uri` -- where pipeline state is persisted; accepts file://,
s3://, or postgres:// URIs. `commit_interval_s` -- how often state is
committed, default 30. `log_format` -- json or text. `on_error` -- stop,
skip, or dead-letter. Connector credentials do not belong here; see the
authentication guides.
row.name: qrv-config-reference

row.content:
# Batching and throughput

Throughput is mostly a function of batch size. Each sink declares a sweet spot
(`batch_rows` on the relational sinks, `batch_bytes` on the object-store
sinks); start there and double it until p99 write latency degrades. Larger
batches amortize per-request overhead but raise retry cost, since a failed
batch is retried whole. The runner's per-stage `records out` counter divided
by wall time is the number to watch.
row.name: qrv-guide-batching

row.content:
# Tuning batch fairness

EmbeddedScheduler assigns batches to workers in the local runner. A slow
transform occupies its worker but does not block assignment of the next batch to
another worker.

The checkpoint interval interacts with fairness. A short interval makes
EmbeddedScheduler pause assignment while a checkpoint is written, so a pipeline
with many small batches sees lower throughput than its CPU headroom would
suggest. Raise the interval before adding workers.
row.name: qrv-tuning-scheduler

row.content:
# Deploying to a fleet

A runner fleet is a pool of worker processes managed by the control plane.
`quorva deploy` uploads a validated pipeline and schedules it; the fleet
assigns stages to workers, restarts failed stages, and exposes status and
metrics. Fleets scale horizontally -- add workers to run more pipelines, not to
make one stage faster.
row.name: qrv-deployment-overview
row.source_description: bench corpus: Deploying to a fleet

row.content:
# Webhook sink

`qv.sinks.WebhookSink(url, *, method="POST", idempotent=False)` posts each
batch to an HTTP endpoint. Because most webhooks are not idempotent, the runner
will not retry a webhook write by default; declare `idempotent=True` only if
the endpoint de-duplicates.
row.name: qrv-sink-webhook

commit_interval_s. checkpoint_store_uri. commit batch. interval seconds. state
store. on_error. dead_letter_uri. schema.mode. schema.ref. retries.max_attempts.
retries.base_delay_ms. log_format. runner. name. Each key is documented on its
own page; this index only lists them.
row.name: qrv-config-index

row.content:
# Sources overview

Built-in sources include files (CSV, JSONL, Parquet), object stores, relational
databases via change-data-capture, and HTTP polling. Every source implements
offset tracking so the runner can resume from the last committed position.
Custom sources subclass `qv.Source` and implement `read_batch` and
`current_offset`.
row.name: qrv-sources-overview

row.content:
# Delivery guarantees

Quorva provides effectively-once delivery: each record's effect reaches the
destination a single time, even across crashes and restarts. The runner
commits source offsets and sink acknowledgments together; after a failure it
resumes from the last committed state, and re-submits only batches the sink
never acknowledged. Sinks that declare idempotent writes make the re-submission
safe; for the rest, the runner uses a transactional two-phase commit where the
backend supports it.
row.name: qrv-guide-delivery

row.content:
# Mutual TLS authentication

In mutual TLS the client presents a certificate issued by CertificateAuthority
before any request is accepted. Access tokens are valid for 15 minutes; a client
renews them against the regional edge endpoint. Client certificates rotate every
24 hours, and a certificate older than that is refused.

Every audit record stores the peer_serial of the presented client certificate so
that a request can be traced back to one certificate.
row.name: qrv-auth-mtls

row.content:
# Versioning and compatibility

Quorva follows semantic versioning. The on-disk checkpoint format is stable
within a minor release; a major release may change it and ships a migration
note. The Python API's v1 surface is maintained through the 1.x line; v2 is the
current surface. Pin the minor version in production.
row.name: qrv-versioning-policy

# BigQuery sink

`qv.sinks.BigQuerySink(dataset, table, *, idempotent=True)` streams rows into
BigQuery using insert IDs for de-duplication, which is what makes its writes
idempotent and therefore retryable by the runner.
row.name: qrv-sink-bigquery

row.content:
# Security model

Quorva holds no long-lived secrets of its own: connector credentials come from
the process environment, a referenced file, or workload identity on fleet
runners. Pipeline definitions are not secret and may be committed; the values
they reference are resolved at runtime and never written into state or logs.
row.name: qrv-security-overview

row.content:
# Replaying a pipeline

`quorva replay` re-runs a stored range of records against the current pipeline
configuration. Replay is a debugging tool, not a recovery tool: it runs the
pipeline in EphemeralMode, and the run always starts from the beginning of the
requested range.

If you interrupt a replay, restarting it replays the whole range again. Use the
`--to` flag to bound the range when the source is large.
row.name: qrv-cli-replay

row.content:
# CSV source

`qv.sources.CsvSource(path, *, has_header=True, delimiter=",")` reads rows from
a CSV file or glob into records keyed by column name. Offsets are byte
positions, so a run resumes mid-file after a restart. Large files stream; they
are not loaded whole.
row.name: qrv-source-csv

row.content:
# Executing pipelines (v2)

Quorva v2 replaces the method call with a module-level entry point:
`qv.execute(pipeline, *, wait=True, limit=None, state_uri=None)`. `wait`
replaces v1's `blocking`, `limit` replaces `max_records`, and `state_uri`
generalizes `state_dir` to any checkpoint store URI. `qv.execute` returns a
`RunHandle` with `status()`, `wait()`, and `cancel()`.
row.name: qrv-v2-execute

row.content:
# Parallelism

The runner assigns each stage a number of workers; raising a stage's worker
count lets independent batches run at the same time. This helps only when the
stage is the bottleneck and its work is divisible -- a single downstream sink
that serializes writes gains nothing from more upstream workers. Set worker
counts from the per-stage throughput counters, not by guessing.
row.name: qrv-guide-scaling

row.content:
# Kinesis sink

The Kinesis sink publishes records to a stream and relies on the stream's shard
layout. Delivery is at-least-once. Ordering is preserved per shard; records from
different shards have no relative order guarantee.

Default retention is 24 hours, which can be extended on the stream. The maximum
record size is 1 MiB.
row.name: qrv-sink-kinesis

row.content:
# Postmortem: September 2026 cutover loop

On 30 September 2026 a CutoverController oscillated between 40% and 50% traffic
for 22 minutes. The new fleet's error rate exceeded the stable fleet's by 1.8
percentage points, just under the rollback trigger, while p99 latency was 3.4
times the stable fleet's. Latency was not part of the automatic rollback
condition, so the controller kept stepping forward and the operator kept
rolling back manually.

The fix adds a latency ratio to the rollback condition and refuses a manual
rollback within one hold window of the previous one.
row.name: qrv-incident-2026-09-cutover
row.source_description: bench corpus: Postmortem: September 2026 cutover loop

row.content:
# Backpressure and flow control

When a downstream stage cannot keep up, the runner slows the stages feeding it
rather than letting buffers grow without bound. Each buffer has a high-water
mark; when it fills, upstream stages pause until the consumer drains it below
the low-water mark. This applies end to end: a slow destination ultimately
pauses the source itself, so memory stays bounded no matter how fast the input
arrives.
row.name: qrv-guide-backpressure
row.source_description: bench corpus: Backpressure and flow control

row.content:
# CDC slot retention

The PostgresSource uses the logical-replication slot named by its `slot`
argument and confirms its log position once per committed checkpoint; the
database retains WAL segments the slot has not confirmed. While the slot is
live, a run resumes from the confirmed position without re-reading the table.
When a pipeline has not acknowledged a position within `cdc_slot_ttl_hours`
-- default 24 hours -- the slot is released, and the next start performs a
full snapshot instead of resuming.

A pipeline that checkpoints rarely therefore holds WAL longer than a short
commit interval would suggest.
row.name: qrv-guide-cdc-retention
